name: Cimicifuga foetida extract (by mouth)
short: 96-woman trial vs hormones: on the extract, vaginal bleeding 6.5%, breast tenderness 12.9%, a new breast nodule at 2 years; no significant liver change. Black cohosh, other species: liver failure.
text: Human safety data come from reports of a randomised trial, or trials of the same design, in 96 early postmenopausal women in China, who took Cimicifuga foetida extract or one of two oestrogen-progestogen regimens; there was no placebo group, and the reports give different completion numbers, so their counts should not be added together. Over 3 months, breast tenderness was reported by 12.9% (4 of 31) on the extract, compared with 36.7% and 14.3% on the two hormone regimens, and vaginal bleeding by 6.5% (2 of 31), compared with 26.7% and 82.1%. In the longer reports, the extract group had the lowest prevalence of breast tenderness over 12 months, with most participants having mild or no symptoms, and less breast pain than the hormone groups over 6 months; liver and kidney function and components of the metabolic syndrome did not change significantly with the extract, and the womb lining did not thicken significantly over 24 months. On breast ultrasound over 2 years, breast tissue thickness did not change significantly with the extract; new breast nodules appeared after 2 years in one woman on the extract and in two and four women on the hormone regimens, and the authors concluded that none of the treatments increased malignant breast tumours. A study in 60 people with chronic hepatitis B, in which one of two groups took the herb with adefovir and the other adefovir alone, gives no adverse-event data in its abstract. Black cohosh (Cimicifuga racemosa), a different species covered by its own entry, has been associated with serious safety concerns in a systematic review of adverse events, which also found that clinical studies suggest it is safe and that causal attribution is problematic in most case reports; a case report describes subacute liver failure needing a liver transplant; these data are not about Cimicifuga foetida. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
